You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: To start, could you walk me through your last ordinary working day, from the moment you arrived until you left?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine, let's take it smaller. What was the very first thing you did when you got to work yesterday?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. Think of any one task you remember doing recently at work. What was it?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: When you last took a drone out of service for a repair, what happened, step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you usually find out that a drone needs a repair?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned regulators can ask your company to show how drones have been looked after. What do you have to be able to show them?

Interviewee: Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after. I don't know any more about what we must show them.

Interviewer: Thinking back over the last few months, which day at work was the worst for you, and what happened?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work that you double-check yourself, by hand, because you don't fully trust what you're told or shown?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: If a new service came in to support your work, what would worry you most about it?

Interviewee: I don't know what worries me about a new service.

Interviewer: When something has gone wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who gives you work, and who do you pass work on to?

Interviewee: I don't know who gives me work or who I pass work on to.

Interviewer: You said you add new drones to the fleet. What does adding a drone involve for you?

Interviewee: I add new drones to the fleet and set up charging pads at our sites. A company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in payload, battery range, sensors, and charging connectors. Our company has its own charging pads at its own sites, a few dozen of them.

Interviewer: You also mentioned sending drones to charge. How do you decide which drone goes to which charging pad?

Interviewee: I don't know how I decide which drone goes to which charging pad. Our company has a few dozen charging pads at our own sites, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: What happens when you put a drone back into service after a repair?

Interviewee: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I don't know what happens when I put a drone back into service after a repair.

Interviewer: And when a drone is retired, what does that involve?

Interviewee: I retire old drones from the fleet. I don't know what else is involved in retiring a drone.

Interviewer: What does setting up a charging pad at one of your sites involve?

Interviewee: I set up charging pads at our company's sites. We have our own charging pads at our own sites, a few dozen of them. Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable, and pads are never lent to another company.

Interviewer: You said the drone models differ in payload, battery range, sensors, and connectors. Where do those differences cause you trouble in your work?

Interviewee: I don't know where those differences cause trouble in my work.

Interviewer: You said pads are never lent to another company. What else about your fleet or sites must stay inside your company?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. Our company's drones and charging equipment are kept in working order by technicians like me, and we have our own charging pads at our own sites.

Interviewer: When you take a drone out of service, who else is affected by that?

Interviewee: I don't know who else is affected when I take a drone out of service.

Interviewer: How do you keep track today of what has been done to each drone?

Interviewee: I don't know how I keep track of what has been done to each drone. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: What can go wrong when a drone is sent to charge?

Interviewee: I don't know what can go wrong when a drone is sent to charge.

Interviewer: Is there anything about your work, your drones, or your charging equipment that I haven't asked about and that you think I should know?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, adding new drones, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: From your side, what makes a drone fit to go out on a job?

Interviewee: I don't know what makes a drone fit to go out on a job. I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, adding new drones, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: To start, could you walk me through your last ordinary working day, from the moment you started to the moment you finished?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine, let's take it smaller. On your most recent shift, what was the very first thing you did when you sat down to work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. In your own words, what does your job as a dispatcher involve?

Interviewee: As a dispatcher, I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, meaning I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and while software never picks a drone or a way for us, we do want help finding out which of our drones could get to where a job starts.

Interviewer: Think of the last flight you signed off. What did you look at or check before you gave that sign-off?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned that several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones. What happens when two of you want the same drone or the same site?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try a different angle. Tell me about the worst day you've had at work in the last few months — what happened?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Okay. Is there anything in your work today that you double-check by hand because you don't fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Understood. When you imagine a new service coming into your work, what worries you about it?

Interviewee: I worry about closures coming into force while our drones are already in the air, especially since zones and sudden closures can be announced or amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and relay station reports can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the service itself runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours and occasionally crashes.

Interviewer: When a closure comes into force while one of your drones is already in the air, what do you do today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let me ask it differently. Right after something has gone wrong with a flight, what do you need to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Alright. Who hands work to you, and who do you hand work on to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. What do you need to be sure of before you sign off a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said you want help finding out which of your drones could get to where a job starts. What makes that hard to work out today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Beyond what you've mentioned, what else are you afraid a new service might get wrong?

Interviewee: I worry about instruction links to drones and charging equipment being unreliable, where an instruction might get through twice and the sender cannot tell if the first attempt arrived. I also worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, causing reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Additionally, it worries me that the service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours and occasionally crashes, accepting a few minutes of interruption.

Interviewer: What worries you about the server restarting or crashing while you are in the middle of planning or have flights in the air?

Interviewee: I worry because the service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours, while drones are flying, and it occasionally crashes. We accept a few minutes of interruption when this happens.

Interviewer: When the service comes back after one of those interruptions, what do you need to find when you look at it again?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you about sharing this service with other drone companies?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you about several dispatchers planning at the same time for the same sites and drones?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What should I know about your work that I haven't asked about yet?

Interviewee: I plan and run the flights as the licensed person responsible for each one, meaning I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and while several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, software never chooses a drone or a way for us.

Interviewer: Why does it matter to you that software never chooses a drone or a way for you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What leads you to call off a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you about batteries draining faster in cold and wind than planned?

Interviewee: I worry because batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and radios have patchy coverage especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather.

Interviewer: When reports from a drone arrive late, out of order, twice, or not at all, what does that make difficult for you as the person responsible for the flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you most want a new service to help you with?

Interviewee: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.

Interviewer: What decides whether one of your drones could get to where a job starts?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What is one thing a new service must never do?

Interviewee: I worry about a new service choosing a drone or a way for us, as our policy is that software never chooses those things. Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher.

Interviewer: What else must it never do?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: And what must a new service always do, whatever else happens?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you about an instruction to a drone or to charging equipment getting through twice?

Interviewee: I worry about this because the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

Interviewer: What worries you about the information you receive from the fleet technicians or the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: To start, could you walk me through an ordinary working day at the airspace desk, from the moment you begin to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine, let's take something smaller. Think of your last shift: what was the first thing you did when you sat down?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. In your own words, what is the airspace desk there to do?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. My work is for all customer companies, and I have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Think of the last closure you entered: could you take me through it step by step, starting from how you first heard about it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said that after a closure you want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. What does "disruption" mean to you there?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try a different angle. What was the worst day you've had at the desk in the last few months?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work today that you double-check by hand because you don't fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Imagine a new service arrives to support your desk. What would you be afraid it might get wrong?

Interviewee: I worry about closures that can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. I also worry because closures are often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves.

Interviewer: When a closure comes into force while drones from several companies are already in the air, what happens next on your side?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: And when a closure is amended during the day, what is it about that which worries you?

Interviewee: I worry when closures are amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves. I also worry about a closure coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: Suppose something has just gone wrong involving a closure. What do you need to know straight away?

Interviewee: I want to know how much disruption the closure caused across customers.

Interviewer: You also said you have no business looking into any one company's operations. How does that fit with wanting to know the disruption across customers?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Who hands work or information to you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: And who do you hand your work on to, or who depends on what you produce?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned corridors between sites and the zones that group them. What changes in that picture over time, and what do you have to do when it does?

Interviewee: I know the authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. Closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. My notes do not state what changes in the network of flight corridors or zones over time, or what I have to do when it does.

Interviewer: How does a sudden closure differ for you from a planned one?

Interviewee: Planned closures have a start and end time, whereas sudden ones apply at once. Both are announced by the authorities.

Interviewer: In what form do the authorities' announcements reach you, and what do you do with one when it arrives?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Once you know how much disruption a closure caused, what do you use that knowledge for?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What should the customer companies be able to see of the airspace picture you keep?

Interviewee: Customer companies accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone. I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities.

Interviewer: When the authorities announce a closure, what exactly is it that gets closed?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything about your work, or about what you'd need from a new service, that I haven't asked and you'd want me to know?

Interviewee: I keep the shared airspace picture for all customer companies and have no business looking into their operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
